content: The transfusion of blood and its components is a critical, life-saving medical intervention. However, it carries potential risks, including adverse events related to both the donation and transfusion processes. These adverse events encompass reactions, incidents, near misses, errors, deviations from standard procedures, and accidents. Haemovigilance refers to a comprehensive set of surveillance procedures that monitor the entire transfusion chain, from blood donation and processing to its provision, transfusion, and patient follow-up. This system involves the reporting, investigation, and analysis of adverse events, as well as the development and implementation of recommendations to prevent their occurrence or recurrence. The ultimate aim of haemovigilance is to continuously improve the quality of the transfusion chain by implementing corrective and preventive actions, thereby enhancing patient safety, improving donor safety, and reducing waste. Haemovigilance systems should be fully integrated into the quality management frameworks of all institutions involved in blood donation, processing, inventory management, storage, distribution, and clinical transfusion. The structure of a haemovigilance system is largely determined by the national blood and healthcare systems. Such systems rely on the traceability of blood products from donors to recipients and vice versa, as well as the effective monitoring, reporting, investigation, and analysis of adverse events. The management of information generated through haemovigilance is essential for updating blood policies and guidelines, leading to improvements in processes and practices. Establishing a haemovigilance system requires coordination and collaboration among various stakeholders, including ministries of health, blood transfusion services, hospitals, professional organizations, public health institutions, regulatory agencies, and patient and donor groups. Effective leadership, governance, and adequate resources are essential for the development and sustainability of such systems. Haemovigilance should be incorporated into national blood and health policies, with a stepwise approach to its implementation. Key elements of a haemovigilance system include standards and definitions aligned with international recommendations, traceability of blood products, and mechanisms for reporting, investigating, and analyzing adverse events. The system should also include guidelines and procedures for data collection, validation, and analysis, as well as corrective and preventive actions to address identified weaknesses. In the context of blood donation and provision, haemovigilance involves recognizing and managing adverse events associated with donation, implementing policies and protocols for all processes, and conducting epidemiological surveillance of donors. It also includes reporting errors, deviations, and abnormalities in blood products, as well as maintaining communication between blood transfusion services and hospital blood banks. In clinical transfusion, hospitals and healthcare facilities are responsible for recognizing and managing transfusion-related adverse events, ensuring proper identification of patients and blood products, and implementing clinical guidelines for safe transfusion practices. They must also maintain traceability of transfused blood products, respond to product recalls, and participate in hospital transfusion committees. Regular audits of clinical transfusion practices and staff training are essential components of haemovigilance in clinical settings. The Ministry of Health (MoH) holds ultimate responsibility for the national blood system, ensuring the quality, safety, and sufficiency of blood and blood products. The MoH should provide leadership and governance for a national haemovigilance system, including comprehensive surveillance of the transfusion chain, advisory committees with medical and scientific expertise, and adequate resources for system development. The system should be confidential and non-punitive to encourage reporting and foster trust. In summary, an effective haemovigilance system requires collaboration among all stakeholders, integration into institutional quality systems, and adherence to international standards. It plays a vital role in improving the safety of blood donation, transfusion, and patient outcomes while fostering trust and ensuring the sustainability of the national blood system.
